stem: A client presents 90 minutes after sudden focal neurologic deficits and is being considered for reperfusion therapy. Why is urgent brain imaging obtained before treatment?

options.A: Brain imaging is obtained mainly to determine the client's blood type before reperfusion because transfusion compatibility determines eligibility for thrombolysis.
options.B: Brain imaging is obtained mainly to confirm that every ischemic stroke is already visible because absence of an infarct on early imaging excludes acute stroke.
options.C: Brain imaging is essential to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before reperfusion therapy because hemorrhage changes management and would make intravenous thrombolysis inappropriate.
options.D: Brain imaging is used mainly to identify chronic neurologic disease before treatment because excluding acute hemorrhage is unnecessary when onset is witnessed.

rationale: The current 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline requires urgent brain imaging as part of reperfusion evaluation so intracranial hemorrhage can be excluded before thrombolytic treatment. Noncontrast CT is a rapid standard method for detecting acute hemorrhage. C therefore identifies the critical purpose. A is unrelated to brain imaging, B incorrectly requires a visible early infarct, and D incorrectly treats witnessed onset as eliminating the need to exclude hemorrhage.
educational_objective: Recognize urgent brain imaging as essential before acute ischemic-stroke reperfusion therapy to exclude intracranial hemorrhage and guide safe treatment selection.
source_document_title: 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
source_locator: Emergency neuroimaging/reperfusion evaluation recommendations in the 2026 acute ischemic stroke guideline; AHA 2026 guideline hub and clinical resources on imaging before thrombolysis.
source_claim_supported: Urgent brain imaging is required in acute stroke evaluation before reperfusion treatment to distinguish hemorrhage from ischemia and guide thrombolytic eligibility; noncontrast CT is a rapid modality for detecting acute hemorrhage.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation — medical emergencies and acute/complex physiological alterations, detailed content pp. 42-44.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — acute stroke reperfusion evaluation

source_original.stem: A client presents 90 minutes after sudden focal neurologic deficits and is being considered for reperfusion therapy. Why is urgent brain imaging obtained before treatment?

options.A: Brain imaging is obtained mainly to determine the client's blood type before reperfusion, because transfusion compatibility determines eligibility for thrombolysis.
options.B: Brain imaging is obtained mainly to confirm that every ischemic stroke is already visible, because absence of an infarct on early imaging excludes acute stroke.
options.C: Brain imaging is essential to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before reperfusion therapy, because hemorrhage would change management and make thrombolysis unsafe.
options.D: Brain imaging is used mainly to identify chronic neurologic disease before treatment, because excluding acute hemorrhage is not necessary when onset is witnessed.

source_original.rationale: The 2026 AHA/ASA guideline states that brain imaging is essential before reperfusion therapy to exclude intracranial hemorrhage; noncontrast CT can rapidly detect acute bleeding. Option C states that purpose. Option A incorrectly makes blood typing the reason for brain imaging. Option B incorrectly requires a visible early infarct to confirm ischemic stroke. Option D incorrectly says acute hemorrhage need not be excluded when the onset time is known.
source_original.source_detail: AHA/ASA 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke — Emergency brain imaging/reperfusion evaluation: brain imaging is essential before acute reperfusion therapy to exclude intracranial hemorrhage; noncontrast CT rapidly detects acute hemorrhage. AHA/ASA 2026 acute ischemic stroke guideline, current in 2026; currentness rechecked after the July 2026 guideline correction on 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: acute/complex alterations, medical emergencies and pathophysiologic adaptation. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained key and construct. Tightened C from the broad phrase 'make thrombolysis unsafe' to the precise treatment-selection principle that intracranial hemorrhage makes intravenous thrombolysis inappropriate; currentness reverified against the January 2026 AHA/ASA guideline hub.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Acute ischemic stroke imaging before reperfusion
audit_findings.claim_audit: No treatment dose, imaging time target, or advanced-imaging requirement was added; the item tests only hemorrhage exclusion before reperfusion.

distractor_audit.A: Blood typing is not the purpose of brain imaging.
distractor_audit.B: Early ischemia need not always be visible for acute stroke to exist.
distractor_audit.D: Witnessed onset does not remove the need to exclude hemorrhage.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only C explains the essential pre-reperfusion role of imaging.
audit_findings.cueing: All choices address possible reasons for imaging; no second answer.
audit_findings.blueprint: Acute neurologic emergency under Physiological Adaptation.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Verified current guideline status and avoided extrapolating disputed advanced-imaging selection issues raised in July 2026 commentary.
